name: Linen-Expanse
geological_features: Shallow global ocean averaging 200 meters depth
specific_features: White seafloor visible through clear water creating a linen-like appearance from orbit
Massive filter-feeding organisms spanning hundreds of meters
description: Linen-Expanse is a world almost entirely covered by a shallow, crystal-clear global ocean whose white calcium carbonate seafloor gives the planet a pale, fabric-like appearance from orbit. The ocean averages only two hundred meters in depth, with submerged volcanic ridges rising to create scattered chains of reef-like shallows but no true dry land. Light penetrates to the seafloor across most of the planet, sustaining a photosynthetic ecosystem of extraordinary productivity that supports layer upon layer of marine life.

The atmosphere is rich in oxygen, almost uncomfortably so for baseline humans, a product of billions of years of uninterrupted photosynthetic activity. The air smells clean and sharp, carrying salt and the faint sweetness of marine organic compounds. Weather systems are mild due to the thermal buffering of the global ocean, and storms rarely exceed moderate intensity. The horizon is water in every direction, unbroken and white-tinged, stretching to infinity under a sky that seems too blue.

The dominant megafauna are filter-feeders of staggering size, sessile organisms anchored to the volcanic ridges that extend filamentous feeding structures across hundreds of meters of open water. They resemble living nets, translucent and rippling with bioluminescent pulses that may serve communicative functions. Smaller fauna swarm around them in dense clouds, creating a food web centered on these gentle giants. The ecosystem shows no signs of predatory pressure at the macro scale—a world where cooperation and filter-feeding, not competition, drove evolutionary development.

The absence of dry land makes conventional colonization impossible, but the planet's biological wealth has attracted proposals for floating research stations and aquaculture platforms. The filter-feeder organisms produce compounds with promising medical applications, including a protein complex that shows activity against several forms of human cancer. Harvesting these compounds without harming the organisms is the primary technical challenge. Some marine biologists have argued that the filter-feeders' bioluminescent communication patterns show signs of distributed intelligence, a claim that would dramatically complicate any exploitation plans if confirmed.
